# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# A Careful Reading of the Varga and Holm Comment

The comment has two parts that should be judged separately. The re-analysis in sections 1–4 is valuable. It uses the microdata to put numbers on problems that could previously only be suspected, and it uncovers a serious reporting discrepancy. The conclusion, that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact", does not follow from the comment's own numbers. It also ignores the randomised evidence that tells against it, the same Varden trial the comment cites as the field's most reliable source when its findings are negative.

## Arithmetic checks

Most figures hold up:

- **Table 1:** 98.9 − 95.1 = 3.8 points.
- **Hours:** 34.6/40.3 is a 14.1% fall. 34.8/40.4 is a 13.9% fall.
- **Table 2:** 95.1/0.8 gives +18.9%, 98.4/0.859 gives +14.6%, and 95.4/0.861 gives +10.8%.
- **Real revenue:** 1.014/1.041 gives about −2.6%.

Two figures do not hold up.

**The hours decomposition doesn't add up.** Four days at about 8.7 hours (8 scheduled plus 0.7) is about 34.8 hours. Adding 1.6 hours logged on the day off gives about 36.4 hours, not the reported 34.6. Measured against the 8.06-hour baseline day the total is higher still. The components overshoot the total by roughly 2 hours. They may come from different subsets or definitions, but as written they are inconsistent.

**The novelty extrapolation is off.** Energy fell 0.32 SD between months 3 and 6, about 0.107 SD a month. At that rate the remaining 0.29 SD is gone at around month 8.7, not "around month ten". This doesn't change the argument, but it is a sign of imprecision in the section the conclusion leans on most.

## What the comment gets right

**1. The attrition finding is the most important new fact.** The working paper said nine organisations withdrew "during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". According to the microdata, seven withdrew after the reduced schedule began, and six cited workload or inability to maintain output. If so, this is a material misstatement in the original paper, not just a limitation. The Halden authors should respond to it.

**2. The manager-versus-records comparison is persuasive.** Managers' figures exceeded the records in 19 of 23 cases, so the bias is systematic, not noise. The subset's manager-reported mean (98.9) is close to the full sample's (98.7), which suggests the 23 organisations are not unusual on that measure.

**3. The actual-hours correction is well grounded.** It also lines up closely with Varden: Halden's actual hours fell 14.1%, and Varden's case-processing offices fell 13%.

**4. The revenue and sector points are correct.** They match points made against the original paper. The record-based figure for retail (−11.2%) strengthens the sector point, although it rests on only three organisations.

**5. The data note is candid.** The comment states that its corrected estimates describe non-random subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

## Where the comment overreaches

### 1. The abstract misstates what was corrected

The abstract says that "correcting the first three" problems brings the gain down to 10.8%. Attrition, the first problem, is never corrected. Table 2 adjusts only for output measurement and hours.

The abstract also says four problems "account for most of the reported gain". Revenue cannot account for any of a per-hour output gain, because it plays no part in the calculation.

The microdata apparently include month-one and month-two data for the seven organisations that withdrew after starting. If so, an intention-to-treat analysis, or at least worst-case bounds, was possible and would have been the most useful addition. Without it, the attrition argument is a likely direction of bias, not a measured size.

### 2. "Entirely an artifact" contradicts the comment's own results

After correction, the comment's best estimate is a +10.8% gain per actual hour, using record-based output and timesheet hours. The comment does not show that this figure is an artifact. It argues the figure might be novelty. The conclusion moves from "not shown to be durable" to "entirely an artifact", which is a different claim.

The burden-of-proof argument justifies saying the gain is unproven. It does not justify asserting a zero effect.

### 3. It is selective about the Varden trial

The comment calls Varden's counter-stratum result "the most reliable finding in the literature". But Varden's case-processing stratum comes from the same trial, with the same randomisation, record-based output, timesheet hours and registered plan. It found +12.5% per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4).

That design is essentially the one the comment recommends in its final paragraph. It removes the selection and measurement explanations directly. The comment never mentions this result, yet generalises its conclusion to "reduced-hours schemes" as a whole.

The counter stratum also had the wider confidence intervals of Varden's two strata. Calling it the more reliable finding is hard to defend.

### 4. The convergence points the other way

Halden's corrected estimate is about +11% per actual hour, from an uncontrolled study using records and time tracking. Varden's randomised case-processing estimate is about +12.5%. Two studies with different designs and different weaknesses arriving at similar figures is evidence for a real effect in office and case-handling work.

The comment presents the remaining 10.8% as a leftover awaiting explanation. Read alongside Varden, it looks more like the best current estimate. The one threat both studies share is short duration: six and nine months.

### 5. The novelty argument skips the direct test

- **Energy is not output.** Self-reported energy falling does not show that output fell.
- **Output can be checked directly.** The pilot collected the output index monthly, and some organisations have monthly records. The direct test is whether output per hour declined from month 3 to month 6. The comment doesn't run it.
- **Two points cannot establish a trend.** Extrapolating a straight line from two survey readings ignores the obvious alternative that energy is levelling off above baseline.
- **Novelty is weaker in Varden.** Varden staff did not choose the change, which removes the "staff chose and welcomed it" mechanism the comment relies on. Varden also ran three months longer. Novelty is still possible there, but the comment does not engage with it.

### 6. The meetings section mischaracterises Varden

**Varden made no mechanism claim.** It said the analysis "cannot establish a mechanism", labelled it unregistered, and registered a confirmatory test. The comment argues against a claim Varden didn't make.

**"Selected after the results were known" appears inaccurate.** The meetings data were collected in month six, at managers' request, before the nine-month results existed. The analysis was done later, but the data collection was not fitted to the results.

**The standard of evidence is applied unevenly.** The comment dismisses seven offices as unreplicable. It then relies on three retail organisations, and on a straight line through two survey points, for its own claims.

**The meetings explanation does not support "artifact".** In Varden's data, the cut in meetings could plausibly account for most of the per-hour gain. That gain would be real, coming from removing low-value time. It is neither measurement error nor novelty. If anything, it argues that the gain is durable and could be achieved without cutting hours.

### 7. Two kinds of productivity are conflated

The conclusion's "best-supported finding", that reduced hours reduce output where output depends on presence, concerns output per employee. That is not the per-hour claim the rest of the comment disputes. Varden's own Discussion makes this distinction explicitly. The comment runs the two together.

## A smaller point on record-based output

Some of the records counted "billable hours delivered" as output. That measure is tied to hours worked by construction, so it is not independent of the hours denominator. In those organisations it would tend to show little or no per-hour gain, which may push the record-based index down. This doesn't overturn the managers' overstatement, since 19 of 23 is a consistent pattern, but the 3.8-point gap shouldn't be read as precise.

## Overall assessment

| Claim | Assessment |
|---|---|
| Halden's 23.4% is substantially overstated | **Well supported.** About half disappears with record-based output and actual hours, before attrition is even considered. |
| Halden misreported when and why organisations withdrew | **Supported, and serious.** Halden's authors should respond. |
| Reduced hours cut output per employee in coverage-bound work | **Supported**, mainly by Varden. |
| The remaining ~11% gain is novelty | **Possible, not shown.** The direct test, using monthly output, wasn't run. |
| Per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact" | **Not supported.** It contradicts the comment's own residual estimate and Varden's randomised case-processing result. |
| The meetings hypothesis should not be cited | **Mischaracterised.** Varden presented it as a hypothesis and registered a test. |

Read together, the three papers point to a modest picture. In office and case-handling work, the per-hour gain is real but roughly half Halden's headline figure, at about 10–12%. Part of it plausibly comes from cutting low-value time such as meetings. Durability beyond six to nine months is untested. In work that depends on staff being present, output and service fall.

Varden's 24-month follow-up, including the registered meetings test, is the evidence most likely to settle what remains. The comment's methodological recommendations are sound and would apply to that follow-up as well.
